goal: Make a pending $memo read give its promise instead of throwing a not-ready error, and add a React use-like read that unwraps it

claims.text: Current rule: any $memo can hold a promise; a read of a value still loading throws a not-ready error that carries the load, and nothing turns a memo into a promise (named 'as in Solid'). On the client, a memo that reads a loading value keeps its old value and is pending.

Current rule for imperative code: a read never gives a promise or undefined typed as the value; code that waits says so with $resolve(memo, {timeout, signal}); a handler that reads an async memo with no value is BRM182 unless $isPending guards it. Passing the raw promise to handlers (Marko 6) was weighed and rejected because it types the promise as the value; the maintainer chose the explicit wait.

A promise in markup already renders its settled value in text and attributes, makes the nearest #loading pending, and the latest promise wins (maintainer, 2026-10-30, shipped in 0.5.0). A promise prop is a plain promise in the child, and $memo(prop) is how a child gets a pending value.

Usage in the repo: 1301 tracked .brm files; 58 `await $memo` sites, 7 `$resolve(` sites, 19 `$isPending(` sites, 65 `#loading` blocks; $memo appears in .brm files under packages/brumate (170), packages/ui (72), website/ui (27), website/src (8), examples (12), benchmarks (4). NotReady appears 17 times in src (server.ts 9, client/updates.ts 8); 23 test files mention NotReady, $resolve or $isPending; 14 website docs pages mention pending, not-ready or $resolve.

claims.text: React use(promise): reads the value or suspends the component by throwing to the nearest Suspense; can be called conditionally, not in handlers; the promise must be stable across renders (created outside render or cached), otherwise each render makes a new promise and suspends again. A promise in state or props is a plain value.

Marko 6: a promise is a plain value everywhere; only <await> unwraps it; handlers and scripts that read a promise get the promise. Svelte 5 (experimental async, 5.36+): `await` in a component script, in $derived and in markup expressions; a <svelte:boundary> with a pending snippet shows while the first await is pending, and later updates keep the old UI.
Breaking changes in 0.x are minor bumps, and the project ships breaks with no deprecation period; 0.6.0 is planned to carry about 8 features, chosen by the maintainer.

claims.text: 0.6.0 has about 8 slots chosen by the maintainer; P2 is a behavior break while the values-spike/values-build client restructure is approved and pending (J9). Changing read semantics on the client now likely gets reworked by that restructure.

On the client, get() returns a loading memo's promise only when exempt > 0 (update code); at exempt === 0 (handlers, $client callbacks) it throws 'This value is still loading. Wait for it with await $resolve(memo)…', effects throw NotReady and skip, memos that compute throw NotReady. So P2 means removing the exempt === 0 throw and the effect skip, not widening exempt; queued updates (exempt > 0) already read the promise. $resolve's doc says it waits for the load of the current inputs when they change while it waits.

`$effect` never runs on page load, and the server runtime has no effect code (0 matches for 'effect' in server.ts). Today the server triggers a #loading boundary only from reads in markup (and in memos that markup reads), and waits at `await`; an effect cannot trigger a server boundary in the current model. On the client, an effect that reads a loading memo skips the run and runs again when it settles (J10).

Model per Q1 (React shape): a memo whose compute returns a promise, calls a server function or awaits is typed `Promise<T>` at every bare read, in scripts, handlers, effects and markup alike. The type tells the user it is async, which is the maintainer's goal. Markup `{m}` renders it as a promise already renders (J3: settled value, nearest #loading, latest wins). `$use(m)` is the unwrap read, typed T. This supersedes P1-P3: the P3 union goes, since the type is always Promise<T> and `$use` is the only way to a T.

claims.text: A memo that reads another async memo has two honest spellings and the compiler gives each a type. (a) `const b = $memo($use(a) + 1)`: $use inside the compute throws NotReady as a bare read does today, so b is async and typed Promise<number>; dependency tracking and the client's 'keep old value while pending' stay as they are. (b) `$memo(a.then(x => x + 1))` chains the promise by hand, with no throw. A bare `a + 1` in a compute is a type error (Promise + number) and a compile error, which replaces the silent automatic pending. The compiler infers the async type of b from a `$use` of an async memo in its compute, so b is Promise<T> without annotation.

claims.text: Answer to O1 under Promise<T>: `await m` in a handler captures the promise of the inputs at read time, as `await fetch()` does, and it is typed as that, so it is no longer a hidden wrong value. For the latest value the user keeps `await $resolve(m)`, whose doc already waits for the current inputs. The docs say `await m` for a snapshot and `$resolve` for the latest. claims.text: Drop the no-op catch of P13 and its lint claim. The memo hands out a fresh derived promise per read, with no catch attached. A dropped rejected promise is a normal unhandled rejection in the browser (window unhandledrejection), as for any promise in JS. The memo's own error is untouched: it still holds the error, and a $use, a markup read or a #try path throws it as now (decisions.md:128). Nothing is swallowed. claims.text: One pending rule for `{m}`, whatever way m is built: markup waits for the memo's current promise, shows nothing new until it settles, keeps the content already shown on later loads, and makes the nearest #loading pending on the first load (decisions.md:137 and the #loading rule at :27). That is the promise-in-markup rule J3 plus the existing 'later updates keep the content'. The memo's 'keep the old value' for script reads goes: in a script, `$use(m)` while a reload runs suspends (a compute) or skips the run (an effect), and `$isPending(m)` is the only way to see the old state. One spelling in computes: `$use(a)`. Drop the `.then` spelling (b) of P10 as a documented form; it works because it is a promise, but it is not taught. Drop spelling (a)'s 'keeps the old value in scripts' claim.

Names under the model (answer to O11). Go: `$resolve` (7 sites) if the promise handed out by a read follows the latest load of the memo, that is, when inputs change before it settles it settles with the newest value; that is $resolve's rule moved into the read, and it fixes O1 properly instead of leaving a snapshot; BRM182 and pending-reads.ts (392 lines) go with it. Stay: NotReady (17 refs; `$use` is a throw), `await $memo` (58 sites; server schedule point, equal to `$use` at the declaration), `$isPending` (19; a promise cannot say 'reloading with an old value') and `#loading (m)` (65; same). Net: spellings of an async read go from three ($resolve, `await $memo`, $isPending) to three (bare promise, `$use`, `await $memo`) with $isPending a state test, so the names do not shrink, and the runtime does not get smaller. The gain is the type, and the removal of one compile error class. I do not claim more.

The script only treats a call as async when its import resolves to a file with 'use server' in the first 300 bytes; 31 .brm files declare 'use server' inline (23 $memo calls inside them) and are missed. Its argument window stops at the first ');', cutting multi-line computes. A grep for $memo calls to get/load/list/fetch/read-named functions finds 72 lines against 28 detected. 18 files have no </script>, so rfind returns -1 and their script/markup split is wrong. The 15 direct breaks cannot be used as a go figure.

The 76 markup mentions assume `{m}` keeps working, but markup reads of derived memos and attribute/prop uses (J3 covers text and attributes only) are not tested. claims.text: Dropping $resolve by making each read's promise follow the memo's latest load is buildable, but it moves $resolve's machinery into every read, not out of the runtime. client resolve() (updates.ts:405-466, about 60 lines) carries a waiter registry, settle of dirty scopes, loadingUpdates draining, an abort when the scope leaves the page, timeout and signal. A read in markup or a handler would have to create that per read, or the memo cache one shared 'latest' promise (new state per memo on server and client, which P9's size gate at 13.6 kB gz does not yet price). 17 doc/code lines use timeout or signal, so those options need a new spelling (Promise.race by hand) or stay as $resolve, so $resolve does not go. P20 itself says the runtime does not get smaller.

claims.text: P18 says the memo hands out a fresh promise per read; P20 says the promise follows the latest load. Both cannot hold cheaply: a fresh following promise per `{m}` render registers a new waiter on each update, and J3's 'latest promise wins' in markup then sees a new promise identity on every re-render of the same pending load. Identity must be stable per load, which is the shared-state option of O16. The spike needs a test that re-rendering a pending `{m}` twice does not restart #loading or leak waiters.

The kill rule 'inference blind to helpers that return promises' conflicts with P17's own rule that only awaits, 'use server' calls and promise returns count, so any helper miss kills it with no stated sample size. The size gate has no tolerance, and todos has been 13.6 kB only for client code that this spike does not run through the changed read paths until values-build lands. questions.ask: What should the $memo change buy? (a) Handlers can write `await m`: today they write `await $resolve(m)`, which also waits for the current inputs. (b) The React model: an async memo is typed and read as Promise<T> everywhere, markup renders it as it renders promises now, and a `$use(m)` read unwraps it in scripts and render code. This breaks hundreds of bare reads. (c) Only a named suspend point: `$use(m)` marks where render waits, and bare reads stay as they are.
questions.answer: The goal is to simplify async handling and give better type inference: users would know from the type whether a memo is async. With promise-giving memos, an effect that reads an async memo triggers the loading boundary on the server, which leaves two places that can trigger a loading boundary: effects and host markup. The maintainer believes the current memo works the same way. (Closest to option b, the React model, with the motivation being runtime simplicity and types.)

questions.ask: Effects never run on the server or on page load, so an effect cannot trigger a server #loading boundary today, and the new model does not change that. Is the change still worth building if the only boundary trigger stays host markup, with the gain being the Promise<T> type and `$use`?
questions.answer: Not asked; inferred from Q1: the maintainer named type inference as a reason on its own. Whether that gain is worth the measured cost is decided when the maintainer approves debate.md.
